stimulus.text:
President Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925 (verbatim excerpt):

"After all, the chief business of the American people is business. They are profoundly concerned with producing, buying, selling, investing and prospering in the world. I am strongly of opinion that the great majority of people will always find these are moving impulses of our life."

"We make no concealment of the fact that we want wealth, but there are many other things that we want very much more. We want peace and honor, and that charity which is so strong an element of all civilization. The chief ideal of the American people is idealism."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925, public domain (American Presidency Project).

stem: Compared with Progressive Era reformers, Coolidge's view of business was most different in its

options.text: trust in private enterprise over government action
celebration of profit as a public good
options.misconception: Coolidge calls wealth a means, not a public good in itself. The speech praises business, but it stops short of calling profit a good.

options.text: demand for new laws to curb corporations
options.misconception: Coolidge opposed new laws to curb corporations. Demanding such laws was the Progressive position, not his.

options.text: support for labor unions and farm aid
options.misconception: Coolidge did not support labor unions or farm aid. Unions were weak in the 1920s, and farm distress went unanswered.

rationales.A: Background: Progressives used government to curb big business, while Coolidge trusted private enterprise and cut taxes. That trust in business over government is the sharpest difference.
rationales.B: Coolidge calls wealth a means, not a public good in itself. The speech praises business, but it stops short of calling profit a good.
rationales.C: Coolidge opposed new laws to curb corporations. Demanding such laws was the Progressive position, not his.
rationales.D: Coolidge did not support labor unions or farm aid. Unions were weak in the 1920s, and farm distress went unanswered.
rationales.general:
1. Recall the Progressive view: government should curb big business and protect the public.
2. Read Coolidge: business is the chief business of Americans, and wealth serves ideals.
3. Compare the two: the gap is who leads, government or private enterprise.
4. Test the other options: none of them names this shift in trust from government to business.
Remember: to compare two eras, name what each side trusted most and place them side by side.
